In summary, our research is concerned with
the virulence factors of E. coli strain J96, which causes urinary tract infections in man and is also able to cause extraintestinal infections.
the virulence properties of the cloned E. coli genes in different animal infection models.
the virulence properties of E. coli 536 in different animal models, which are relevant for urinary tract infections and septicemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cloned hly determinants of E. coli O18, O6 and O75 and the plasmid pHy152 are equally potent in conferring virulence in a mouse peritoneal infection assay.
S-fimbria and serum resistance are not essential for pathogenicity of uropathogenic O6 E. coli strains in the mouse peritonitis and nephropathogenic assays.
S-fimbria, serum resistance and chromosomally encoded hemolysin are important virulence determinants for uropathogenic Escherichia Coli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hemolysis and serum resistance are important for the virulence of uropathogenic strains in the kidney but are not required for the development of sepsis.
S-fimbria, serum resistance and chromosomal hemolysin contribute to pathogenicity in vivo in a different manner and that their relative importance is dependent on the experimental system used.
S-fimbria-mediated adherence and serum resistance are important in the initial colonization of the host and that hemolysin is a major determinant in the subsequent spread of the bacteria in the host.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the virulence of the E. coli strain O6:K15 in the mouse peritonitis assay is due to the hemolysin gene hlyA and that the S-fimbria-mediated adhesion to uroepithelial cells and the serum-resistance of this uropathogenic strain have no influence on virulence in the peritonitis model.
the virulence of uropathogenic strains is not dependent on a single virulence determinant but is the sum of different virulence factors.

the virulence properties of uropathogenic strains of E. coli can differ significantly in different animal models, and that the virulence of the strain 536 is dependent on S-fimbria, serum resistance and the chromosomally encoded hemolysin.
